doc.title: Keter Betts interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 11, 1996

title: Learning jazz versus classical bass: playing what you think
summary: His classical bass teacher was amazed by jazz improvisation; Betts explains playing what you hear and treating the instrument as an extension of the mind.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Let me back track just a little bit. When you were first learning the bass, in addition to learning the technique of it, what was the — how did you learn the jazz repertory? Was it just picking up music from your teacher?

No, no, no. Because the teacher there was strictly classical. And he would have, even when Red would come in, the first thing he would do is have you play, he’d say, “just play me one chorus of ‘Body and Soul.’” And you know he’d say I just don’t understand how you do that. Because you use the imagination. See the difference between — the fine line between that is if you’re studying classical, strictly classical, you are actually taught to play what you see. In other words what is written out, you play what you see. So you become, this is your guide. And when you’re playing jazz, I mean if you’re not reading something, you have to play what you think. So it’s the complete opposite. You have to think. And then when it comes to solos, that’s when you can tell good soloists and bad soloists is how well they think. I show students, when you really get down to the nitty gritty part of it is the fact that you’re learning the instrument, you’re trying to learn the instrument to a certain point as well as you know your body. In other words, let’s say if you were itching, and you had something in your hand and you were itching on the shoulder, you would say, “Keter, scratch on my shoulder.” And you say, “no, no, a little further over, a little further down.” But now if you could do it you could put your hand right on it. So this is the way that you approach the bass, that you put your hand right on what you hear in your mind, if you hear it. And then you’ll find out that you’re actually, I mean when you’re standing there with the bass, it looks like two things, but it’s really one because of the fact that it’s a person’s mind that’s coming out of the instrument. So consequently what is happening is the person is not playing the instrument, he’s playing themself. Because you go inside the instrument and you play out.
That’s a great way to say it.
It’s not too heavy for you this early in the morning, is it?
No, I like it. I might have to listen to it again later to make sure I got it all man.
